title: Jacquet refuses to play with him; the 1967 Austin three tenors concert
summary: Cobb says Jacquet declined a battle of music, and recalls the 1967 Austin date with Jacquet and Buddy Tate, praising Tate.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Oh yeah, he's original; he's got good ideas. He ain't no slouch. he can play. But I'm gonna say this, and I hope it gets back to him --he don't want never wanted to play with me, and we've had all the opportunities to play together to make money as a commercial situation, but he refuses. My right man here in the club wanted him down here and I tried to get him to New York; nobody answered his phone and I wanted to talk to him personally myself. When I had my 7-piece group, he had his, I said, "Man, we are a controversy out here as the two Texas tenor saxophone players - let's go out and capitalize on it and make some money with a Battle of Music. What difference does it make what they say about who is the greatest. Does it make any difference to you?" "Oh, no, no man." "Good, "Then we'll do it." But it never materialized. It was just conversation. A man in Chicago called me and here's a man that could sit up here and tell you now -- from the Jazz (Joe Segal - ed.) showcase, to put me and him together, and I gave him my price and called Illinois and asked him, he said he didn't want to play with nobody; he'd play with his own group. But he don't want to play with me. Don't call my name, for him to play, and here we were in Houston, and grew up together. Same high school band, everything. But he won't play with me -- not after '67, when George Reed and Longhorn Texas situation in Austin, and put us together. Since then, he don't want to be bothered with me.

'67. I was working the Cafe Animal and my boss gave me the Sunday (phonetic) and I went to Austin, and it was on the set with Joe Jones, on drums, Illinois Jackson, me and Buddy Tate -- three Texas tenors.

And I put my best foot forward. You know why? Because of the thing we talked about prior to New York before I moved back to Texas and it never materialized -- I said, "I'm gonna show you how this thing could really go." That was what I was saying to myself, now. And ... I can lay down and be lazy, I could get up and play -- but you know, there ain't nobody that great. So you got to let people know.
Buddy is my man. My right hand man. Ain't gonna find a better guy than Buddy Tate anywhere you go. He called me four o'clock one morning; I said, "Man, what ...
